title: Cache Policies & Performance
summary: When a cache set fills up, something must decide what stays, what leaves, and when writes hit memory. Learn the policies and the math behind cache speed.

blocks.markdown:
A cache is small, so it fills up fast. Two questions then matter: **what gets evicted**, and **when do writes reach memory**?

- **Replacement policy** decides which line to kick out when a set is full.
- **Write policy** decides when a written value reaches main memory.
- Together they shape hit rate and speed. See [cache-fundamentals](cache-fundamentals).

blocks.subTitle: Key terms
blocks.markdown:
Terms used throughout this topic.

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Hit / miss | Data found / not found in cache |
| Eviction | Removing a line to make room |
| Dirty bit | Flag: line changed since loaded |

Every policy below is really just an answer to "what happens on a miss?"

blocks.subTitle: LRU
blocks.markdown:
When a **set** (the group of lines a memory address can map to) is full, the cache must evict one line to fit a new one.

**LRU (Least Recently Used)** evicts the line that hasn't been touched for the longest time.

- Matches real access patterns well — recently used data tends to be reused.
- Needs extra bookkeeping (timestamps or a use-order list) per set.

blocks.subTitle: FIFO and Random
blocks.markdown:
Two simpler alternatives to LRU.

- **FIFO (First In, First Out)** — evicts the oldest-loaded line, regardless of recent use. Cheap, but can evict something still needed.
- **Random** — picks any line to evict. Surprisingly close to LRU in practice, and needs zero tracking.

Hardware often picks random or pseudo-LRU for speed, not textbook-perfect LRU.

blocks.subTitle: Write-through vs write-back
blocks.markdown:
When a CPU writes data, when does main memory actually get updated?

| Policy | Memory updated |
|---|---|
| Write-through | Immediately, on every write |
| Write-back | Only when the line is evicted |

Write-back is faster (fewer memory trips) but needs a **dirty bit** — a flag marking "this line changed and must be written back before eviction."

blocks.subTitle: The dirty bit
blocks.markdown:
The **dirty bit** is one bit per cache line, set to 1 the moment write-back data is modified.

- Clean line evicted → just overwrite it, memory already matches.
- Dirty line evicted → write it back to memory first, then overwrite.

This is why write-back needs extra state that write-through never bothers with.

blocks.subTitle: Write-allocate vs no-write-allocate
blocks.markdown:
A **write miss** (writing to data not in the cache) needs its own rule too.

- **Write-allocate** — load the line into the cache, then write. Pairs naturally with write-back.
- **No-write-allocate** — write straight to memory, skip the cache. Pairs naturally with write-through.

Matching the pair avoids pointless cache traffic.

blocks.subTitle: The three Cs
blocks.markdown:
Every cache miss falls into one of three causes.

| Type | Cause |
|---|---|
| Compulsory | First-ever access to that data |
| Capacity | Cache too small to hold the working set |
| Conflict | Too many addresses map to the same set |

Compulsory misses are unavoidable; capacity and conflict misses shrink with a bigger or more associative cache.

**AMAT (Average Memory Access Time)** boils cache performance into one number.

```
AMAT = Hit time + Miss rate × Miss penalty
```

- **Hit time** — cycles to get data already in cache.
- **Miss rate** — fraction of accesses that miss.
- **Miss penalty** — extra cycles to fetch from the next level down on a miss.

blocks.subTitle: A tiny example
blocks.markdown:
Hit time 1 cycle, miss rate 5%, miss penalty 100 cycles:

```
AMAT = 1 + 0.05 × 100 = 6 cycles
```

Even a small miss rate costs a lot, since each miss is ~100x an ordinary hit. This is why shaving miss rate matters more than shaving hit time.

blocks.subTitle: Associativity
blocks.markdown:
**Associativity** is how many lines in a set an address can go to (direct-mapped = 1, fully associative = any line).

- Higher associativity → fewer **conflict misses**, since addresses have more places to land.
- Cost: more comparisons per lookup, so hit time creeps up.

Most real caches settle at 4-way to 16-way as the sweet spot.

blocks.subTitle: Line size
blocks.markdown:
**Line size** is how many contiguous bytes are pulled in together on one miss.

- Bigger lines → fewer **compulsory misses** (neighboring data arrives pre-fetched for free).
- Too big → wastes bandwidth on unused bytes and raises conflict misses (fewer, bigger lines per set).

Typical line sizes: 32–64 bytes.

blocks.subTitle: Cache size
blocks.markdown:
**Cache size** is the total capacity available.

- Bigger cache → fewer **capacity misses**, since more of the working set fits.
- Diminishing returns: doubling size rarely halves misses, and bigger caches are slower and pricier per byte.

This tradeoff is why chips use multiple cache levels (L1 small/fast, L3 large/slower).

Caches reward **locality** — reusing data that's already nearby in memory or time.

- **Spatial locality** — access memory in order (loop over an array, not a linked list) so line-size fetches pay off.
- **Temporal locality** — reuse a value soon after loading it, before it's evicted.

Same algorithm, cache-friendly layout, can run several times faster. See [performance-analysis](performance-analysis).

Same job, three different amounts of bookkeeping.

Common mistakes:

- **"LRU is always best."** It costs bookkeeping; random or pseudo-LRU is often close enough and cheaper in hardware.
- **"Write-back is strictly better."** It's faster but leaves memory stale until eviction — a problem for other cores or devices reading memory directly.
- **"Bigger cache always helps."** Returns diminish, and a bigger cache can be slower per access.

blocks.subTitle: Write-through vs write-back
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Write-through vs write-back — what's the tradeoff?**

Write-through writes to memory on every store, so memory is always current but every write pays memory latency. Write-back only writes on eviction, tracked with a dirty bit — far fewer memory writes, but memory can be stale until then, which matters for multi-core coherence.

blocks.subTitle: The three Cs
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What are the three Cs of cache misses?**

Compulsory (first touch of that data, unavoidable), capacity (working set doesn't fit, fixed by a bigger cache), and conflict (too many addresses share a set, fixed by more associativity). Naming which C applies shows you understand *why* a miss happened, not just that it did.

blocks.subTitle: Computing AMAT
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is AMAT and how do you compute it?**

AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty. It's the expected cycles per memory access once misses are averaged in. With multiple cache levels, the miss penalty of one level is itself the AMAT of the next level down, chained together.

blocks.subTitle: What is LRU
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is LRU and why use it?**

Least Recently Used evicts whichever cache line hasn't been accessed in the longest time, betting that recently used data will be reused soon (temporal locality). It tracks access order per set, which costs hardware — many real chips approximate it (pseudo-LRU) instead of implementing it exactly.

blocks.subTitle: Cache-friendly code
blocks.markdown:
**Q: How do you write cache-friendly code?**

Access memory sequentially so spatial locality pays off (arrays over linked lists, row-major loop order matching row-major storage), and reuse hot data quickly so it survives before eviction. Both cut miss rate without touching the algorithm's complexity.
